High schoolers join university walkouts in major cities and several smaller locations amid urge to fight against racism Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast They came yelling chants that “racists” weren’t “welcome here”, with signs deriding Pauline Hanson’s former fish and chip shop and the One Nation leader herself. On Thursday, thousands of students across the country put down the textbooks to walk through streets in protest against the rise of Pauline Hanson, joining the protests organised by the National Union of Students. When Kaylee, who is in Year 8 and uses they/them pronouns, had asked for the day off school, their mum had requested they lay out their reasoning. They presented her with a four-page essay.

They aren’t a political family; their mum doesn’t regularly read the news, but Kaylee said “I persuaded her” to come along. “People of a different race shouldn’t lose their rights,” Kaylee said. “And queer people have already had a lot of issues with fighting for their rights, and if that gets taken away too, that’s not okay.” Asked why they thought Hanson should not be in charge, Kaylee simply said: “I just don’t think she should be able to make those kinds of choices”. The themes from the speakers were clear - racism is not welcome here, and Hanson does not represent Australia’s youth. Former Victorian Greens leader Samantha Ratnam told the crowd she was impressed by the turnout, saying, “It gives me hope that we can stop the rise of One Nation. Everything is on the line right now.”

At one point, right-wing self-proclaimed journalist Avi Yemini turned up, surrounded by large men wearing all black and another man in a One Nation T-shirt. He tried to make his way into the crowd before being turned around by marshals. As Yemini started filming on the sidelines, a group of students ran into the background to chant “fuck Pauline Hanson”. A few meters away, a parent, Chris, said he can remember walking out of school to strike against Hanson almost 30 years ago, and now he stood with his 13-year-old daughter, Charlie. “I think that everyone should have the same rights and everyone should be able to be treated the same way,” Charlie said.

payload.title: Tuhannet opiskelijat marssivat Australiassa Pauline Hansonia vastaan
payload.summary: Koululaiset liittyivät yliopisto-opiskelijoiden ulosmarsseihin eri puolilla Australiaa. Mielenosoituksissa vastustettiin Pauline Hansonin ja One Nationin nousua sekä puolustettiin yhdenvertaisia oikeuksia.
payload.content:
Tuhannet opiskelijat poistuivat torstaina oppitunneilta eri puolilla Australiaa osoittaakseen mieltään Pauline Hansonin ja tämän johtaman One Nation -puolueen nousua vastaan. Yliopisto-opiskelijoiden ulosmarsseihin liittyi myös koululaisia, ja suurissa kaupungeissa sekä useilla pienemmillä paikkakunnilla järjestettyjen protestien keskeinen viesti oli rasismin torjuminen.

## Koululaiset liittyivät ulosmarsseihin

Protestit järjesti Australian kansallinen opiskelijaliitto. Osallistujat marssivat kaduilla ja huusivat, etteivät rasistit ole tervetulleita. Kylteissä arvosteltiin Hansonia, ja puhujien mukaan hän ei edusta Australian nuoria.

Mukana ollut kahdeksatta luokkaa käyvä Kaylee kertoi valmistelleensa äidilleen nelisivuisen kirjoituksen perustellakseen, miksi halusi jäädä pois koulusta ja osallistua mielenosoitukseen. Kayleen mukaan eri taustoista tulevien ihmisten ei pidä menettää oikeuksiaan. Hän nosti esiin myös seksuaali- ja sukupuolivähemmistöjen oikeuksien puolustamisen.

Kaylee sanoi, ettei hänen perheensä tavallisesti seuraa politiikkaa tai uutisia aktiivisesti. Nelisivuisen perustelun jälkeen hän sai kuitenkin äitinsä lähtemään mukaansa. Opiskelijoiden osallistuminen merkitsi koulupäivän keskeyttämistä, vaikka heitä oli kehotettu pysymään oppitunneilla.

## Oikeudet nousivat puheiden ytimeen

Victorian vihreiden entinen johtaja Samantha Ratnam sanoi osallistujamäärän antavan hänelle toivoa siitä, että One Nationin nousu voidaan pysäyttää. Ratnamin mukaan tilanteessa on nyt ”kaikki pelissä”. Hänen puheenvuoronsa toisti protestien keskeisiä teemoja: rasismia ei hyväksytä, eikä Hanson edusta nuorten Australiaa.

Yhdessä protestissa paikalle saapui oikeistolainen, itseään toimittajaksi kutsuva Avi Yemini seurueineen. Hän yritti päästä väkijoukkoon, mutta järjestyksenvalvojat käännyttivät hänet takaisin. Kun Yemini kuvasi tapahtumaa sivummalta, opiskelijaryhmä ryhtyi huutamaan Hansonin vastaista iskulausetta.

Mielenosoitukseen osallistunut Chris kertoi lähteneensä itsekin koulusta lakkoon Hansonia vastaan lähes 30 vuotta sitten. Nyt hän oli paikalla 13-vuotiaan tyttärensä Charlien kanssa. Charlie tiivisti osallistumisensa perusteluksi yhdenvertaisuuden: kaikilla pitäisi olla samat oikeudet ja kaikkia pitäisi kohdella samalla tavalla.

High schoolers join university walkouts in major cities and several smaller locations amid urge to fight against racism Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast They came yelling chants that “racists” weren’t “welcome here”, with signs deriding Pauline Hanson’s former fish and chip shop and the One Nation leader herself. On Thursday, thousands of students across the country put down the textbooks to walk through streets in protest against the rise of Pauline Hanson, joining the protests organised by the National Union of Students. When Kaylee, who is in Year 8 and uses they/them pronouns, had asked for the day off school, their mum had requested they lay out their reasoning. They presented her with a four-page essay.

They aren’t a political family; their mum doesn’t regularly read the news, but Kaylee said “I persuaded her” to come along. “People of a different race shouldn’t lose their rights,” Kaylee said. “And queer people have already had a lot of issues with fighting for their rights, and if that gets taken away too, that’s not okay.” Asked why they thought Hanson should not be in charge, Kaylee simply said: “I just don’t think she should be able to make those kinds of choices”. The themes from the speakers were clear - racism is not welcome here, and Hanson does not represent Australia’s youth. Former Victorian Greens leader Samantha Ratnam told the crowd she was impressed by the turnout, saying, “It gives me hope that we can stop the rise of One Nation. Everything is on the line right now.”

At one point, right-wing self-proclaimed journalist Avi Yemini turned up, surrounded by large men wearing all black and another man in a One Nation T-shirt. He tried to make his way into the crowd before being turned around by marshals. As Yemini started filming on the sidelines, a group of students ran into the background to chant “fuck Pauline Hanson”. A few meters away, a parent, Chris, said he can remember walking out of school to strike against Hanson almost 30 years ago, and now he stood with his 13-year-old daughter, Charlie. “I think that everyone should have the same rights and everyone should be able to be treated the same way,” Charlie said.
